standard.title: Target language sound system
standard.description: recognise and use features of the target language sound system, including pitch, rhythm, stress, pronunciation and intonation, and demonstrate understanding of how these are represented in familiar contexts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students enter the Y7-10 sequence with no formal prior study of the target language sound system. They bring awareness of English phonology and may have incidental exposure to the target language's sounds. They have not yet systematically learned the phonological features of the target language or how these are represented in its writing system.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise and use the key features of the target language sound system — vowels, consonants, intonation patterns, stress and pitch — and demonstrate understanding of how these are represented in familiar written and spoken contexts.

nodes.label: Target language vowel and consonant sounds
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise and produce the key vowel and consonant sounds of the target language, including those that differ from English.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and attempt to produce at least three target language sounds that differ from English equivalents; recognise these sounds when heard.
nodes.typical_width: Distinguish and produce the full vowel set of the target language; recognise and practise consonant sounds that differ from English; use rhymes, tongue twisters or choral reading to build phonological accuracy.
wider: Compare the vowel systems of the target language and English — map similarities and differences using a visual reference
Research and practise regional pronunciation variations within the target language — identify at least one sound that varies across communities
nodes.hinge_reason: Vowel and consonant accuracy underpins all spoken production. Students who do not develop accurate sound discrimination early will produce habituated errors that are progressively harder to correct as automaticity develops. EU01's pronunciation and intonation demands cannot be met without a phonological foundation.

response_modes.reason: Phonological accuracy is a fluency issue — students often understand the difference between sounds but produce them inconsistently. Repeated, corrective oral practice (choral work, minimal pairs, recording and listening back) builds the muscular habit that underpins accurate production.

success_criteria: Can identify at least three target language sounds that differ from English and attempt to produce them accurately
Can recognise target language vowel sounds when heard in isolation and in words

nodes.label: Intonation and sentence melody
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise and use appropriate intonation patterns for statements, questions and exclamations in the target language.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate at least two distinct intonation patterns (e.g. statement vs question) in spoken target language production.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise and use intonation patterns for statements, questions and exclamations; transcribe spoken texts using intonation cues; use intonation variation in role-play and spoken tasks.
wider: Listen to and compare intonation in audio texts from different target language communities — identify where melody differs from Australian English
Record own spoken target language production and compare intonation with a model — identify specific differences and practise correction

response_modes.reason: Intonation awareness deepens through exposure to varied spoken texts — single sentence drills do not build the sensitivity to sentence melody that natural conversation requires. A range of spoken contexts (announcements, conversations, instructions) builds the broader phonological awareness needed.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Intonation is culturally variable and affects meaning-making in ways that vocabulary and grammar alone do not. Students who develop sensitivity to target language intonation patterns early demonstrate noticeably more authentic spoken production across the secondary sequence.
success_criteria: Can produce audibly different intonation patterns for a statement and a question in the target language
Can identify the intonation pattern used in a short spoken text when listening

nodes.label: Stress, rhythm and phonological representation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise and apply stress and rhythm patterns in the target language and understand how phonological features are represented in the writing system.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify word stress in at least five familiar target language words; demonstrate awareness of how stress or accent marks are represented in writing.
nodes.typical_width: Apply word stress and sentence rhythm in spoken production; use phonological notes or accent marks to support pronunciation; connect phonological representations in writing (e.g. accent marks, diacritics, special characters) to their sound values.
wider: Use phonetic notation or personal phonological notes to support the pronunciation of unfamiliar words — develop a personal pronunciation guide for challenging sounds
Practise stress and rhythm through performance texts (poems, tongue twisters, songs) and reflect on how stress choices affect meaning or emphasis

response_modes.reason: Stress, rhythm and phonological representation draw together the vowel/consonant knowledge from node 1 and the intonation awareness from node 2 into a unified understanding of spoken production. Performance contexts — recitation, role-play, recorded tasks — are the natural integration point.

success_criteria: Can identify word stress correctly in at least five familiar target language words
Can connect at least one phonological feature of the writing system (e.g. accent mark, diacritic, special character) to its sound value
